name: Woodford Folk Festival
season_note: DATE-LOCKED: 27 Dec 2026 – 1 Jan 2027, six days, one hour north of Brisbane. This is exactly the trip window but collides head-on with the Sydney NYE hard anchor — one or the other, not both. Summer storms are near-certain; Woodfordia is a mud festival as often as a dust one. 2026/27 tickets run roughly A$25 (single session) to A$745 (full festival + camping), vehicle parking A$10–80.
why_rated: The single biggest counter-culture gathering in Australia and the one QLD event that is unambiguously hers: 2,000+ performers, 450+ acts, a purpose-built festival village, all-night fire event on New Year's Day, plus debates, workshops, circus and a permanent hippie township feel. People plan whole Decembers around it.

name: Earth Frequency Festival
season_note: WRONG SEASON — the festival has moved to spring: EFF 2026 runs 23–26 October 2026, before the couple lands. No 2027 date announced as of Aug 2026, and it has historically been a Feb event, so there is an outside chance it swings back into the window — worth one check of earthfrequency.com.au in Nov 2026 before writing it off.
why_rated: South-east Queensland's flagship transformational/doof festival — psytrance, bass, dub, techno plus workshops, healing area and market village, the closest thing QLD has to Rainbow Serpent. Would be the top pick of the trip for her if the dates ever line up.

name: Eumundi Markets
season_note: WEEKDAY-LOCKED: Wednesdays 8am–2pm and Saturdays 7am–2pm, every week of the year rain or shine. Go early — by 11am in January it is 32°C under canvas and heaving with school-holiday crowds.
why_rated: One of the largest artisan markets in the southern hemisphere and the anchor of the Sunshine Coast's hippie belt: 500+ stalls of handmade craft, independent fashion, art, tie-dye, crystals, street performers and food carts, 20km inland from Noosa. Consistently the first thing locals name when asked what is worth the drive.

name: Crystal Waters Permaculture Ecovillage, Conondale
region: QLD — Sunshine Coast hinterland / Mary Valley
season_note: Open year-round; the creeks and swimming holes are at their best after summer rain, which is also when the mozzies and leeches arrive. The monthly village market is DATE-LOCKED (one Saturday a month) — check the date before building a day around it. Camping and EcoPark cabins available; hot and humid in January but the Mary River headwaters are swimmable.
why_rated: The world's first intentional permaculture village (est. 1987) — 640 acres, 250 residents, 83 one-acre plots, wildlife sanctuary listing, guided permaculture tours, yoga, sound immersion, a plant-based Friday bistro with live music and a village-green café. A working hippie utopia you can actually stay in, 26km from Maleny and Woodford. Pairs naturally with a Woodford Festival stay.

name: Springbrook NP & Natural Bridge glow worms
season_note: Summer is the BEST glow-worm season — warm humid nights are when the colony is densest, and the waterfalls into the cave actually run. Park entry and the cave are free if you self-drive at dusk; guided 3-hour night tours from Surfers run roughly A$70–95pp. Mountain roads are narrow, unlit and slick after afternoon storms — self-driving back down at 9pm in the wet is the real cost.
why_rated: Gondwana Rainforests World Heritage plateau 45 min from the beach: Purling Brook Falls circuit, Twin Falls, the Best of All Lookout, and a collapsed volcanic cave at Natural Bridge holding the largest concentration of glow worms in Australia. The number-one 'do this instead of the theme parks' answer on Gold Coast forums.

name: Lamington NP — Binna Burra & Green Mountains
region: QLD — Gold Coast hinterland / Scenic Rim
season_note: 1,000m altitude makes it 5–8°C cooler than the coast — a genuine summer heat escape. But it is also the wettest time: leeches on every track, afternoon thunderstorms, and the 21.4km Border Track is a slog in the wet. O'Reilly's access road is 35km of narrow mountain switchbacks with roadworks; Binna Burra is the easier drive.
why_rated: 160km of tracks through Antarctic beech and subtropical rainforest, the free O'Reilly's Tree Top Walk (nine suspension bridges, a 30m fig-canopy deck), regent bowerbirds that land on your hand, and waterfall circuits people rank above anything else in SE QLD. A Saturday shuttle (A$35pp) lets you walk the Border Track one-way.

name: Tamborine Mountain
season_note: Cooler than the coast and green in summer; Curtis Falls actually flows. Gallery Walk gets bumper-to-bumper on summer weekends and school holidays. The commercial Glow Worm Caves and Rainforest Skywalk both charge entry (~A$20–30pp) — the free Curtis Falls and Cedar Creek Falls walks are the better-value half of the day.
why_rated: The soft-option hinterland day: Gallery Walk's arts-and-craft strip, distillery/brewery/cheese cellar doors, Curtis Falls, the Rainforest Skywalk, and hang-glider views over the whole Gold Coast. Half the drive of Lamington for a decent share of the payoff.

name: Burleigh Heads — headland walk, Tallebudgera Creek & Burleigh Pavilion
season_note: Peak summer, peak crowds, peak heat — but this is the right season for it. Tallebudgera Creek is calm, clear and shark-net-free swimming; the headland circuit is best at 6am or after 5pm to dodge 33°C and UV14. No stingers this far south. Storm swells can shut the point for a day or two.
why_rated: The Gold Coast that locals actually use: a free 2.3km rainforest-and-ocean headland circuit in Burleigh Head NP with dolphins off the point, one of Australia's best right-hand point breaks, and a creek mouth people call the best family swim on the coast. Burleigh is the antidote to Surfers Paradise and it costs nothing.

name: Currumbin Rock Pools & Currumbin Valley
season_note: Summer is when the pools are worth it — cold clear mountain water, 25 min inland from Palm Beach. Free, with BBQs and toilets. January means the carpark fills by 9am and the valley road is a single lane in places; flash-flood risk after heavy rain, so skip it the day of a storm.
why_rated: The Gold Coast's worst-kept local secret — a chain of granite swimming holes in the hinterland with rope swings and shaded picnic flats, free, and a completely different world from the beach strip 20 minutes away. Currumbin Valley also carries the coast's alternative-community streak (organic farms, the Ecovillage at Currumbin).

name: Gold Coast market & night-market circuit (Miami Marketta, Village Markets, Currumbin Sanctuary Markets)
season_note: WEEKDAY-LOCKED, and the locks differ: Miami Marketta Wed/Fri/Sat from 5pm (free entry, undercover so storm-proof); Burleigh Farmers Markets Saturday 7am–noon; The Village Markets Burleigh on selected Sundays; Currumbin Sanctuary Markets Friday 4–9pm. Their Byron/Gold Coast window of 27 Jan–2 Feb 2027 covers at least one of each — worth pinning the day.
why_rated: The maker/hippie layer of the Gold Coast that the theme-park brochures hide: a covered laneway of global street food with free live music, independent designers and vintage sellers at Burleigh, and a Friday night market on the Currumbin Wildlife Sanctuary village green. Cheap, atmospheric, and squarely her taste.

name: Coolangatta, Snapper Rocks & Point Danger
season_note: Prime season, and it sits right on the road between Byron and the Gold Coast — near-zero detour cost during their 27 Jan–2 Feb southern window. Summer cyclone swells from the Coral Sea are what make the Superbank fire; they also make it unswimmable for a couple of days at a time. Flagged beaches only.
why_rated: The Superbank at Snapper Rocks is one of the longest sand-bottom right-handers on earth and even non-surfers rate watching it. Rainbow Bay and Greenmount are calm, patrolled, and cheaper to stay near than anywhere further north; Point Danger's captain-Cook memorial straddles the state line so you can stand in two states and two time zones.

name: Currumbin Wildlife Sanctuary
season_note: Open year-round; go at opening because the animals and the humans both wilt by midday in January humidity. Not-for-profit and runs the region's wildlife hospital, so the entry fee reads better than a theme park's.
why_rated: The lorikeet feeding is a Gold Coast institution (wild rainbow lorikeets swarming for a plate of nectar, twice daily since 1947) and it is the only easy way to see koalas, cassowaries, Tassie devils and a working wildlife hospital in one place on the southern coast. Consistently rated above the big theme parks by adult travellers.

name: Gold Coast theme parks (Movie World / Dreamworld / Sea World / Wet'n'Wild)
season_note: Technically open and fully operating, but January is the single worst time: Australian school holidays run to late January, so queues are at their annual peak in 33°C and high humidity. Multi-park passes (~A$120–190pp) only pay off across 2–3 days. Wet'n'Wild is the one that actually improves in the heat.
why_rated: Included for completeness because they are the Gold Coast's headline product and a bought multi-park pass is the cheapest per-day way in. Forum consensus for a budget-conscious adult couple is emphatically 'skip them, do the hinterland' — capture and let them reject it.

name: Magic Millions Carnival & beach barrier draw, Surfers Paradise
season_note: DATE-LOCKED and the dates fall just BEFORE their Gold Coast window: carnival 6–18 Jan 2027, beach barrier draw Tue 7 Jan from 6am on the Surfers Paradise foreshore (horses gallop on the sand ~8am), raceday Sat 11 Jan. They are scheduled to be in Cairns/Port Douglas 18–31 Jan, so this only works if the itinerary shuffles.
why_rated: The barrier draw is free, on the beach at sunrise, and even people who dislike racing rate it as spectacle — thoroughbreds galloping through surf with the high-rises behind. Tagged sport: minor interest, one-sided pick — worth an hour if the calendar happens to land there, never worth moving the itinerary for.

name: Australia Day at HOTA, Gold Coast
season_note: DATE-LOCKED: 26 Jan 2027, afternoon into evening, free entry at the HOTA Outdoor Stage with live music and fireworks. Directly serves the soft Australia Day anchor — and 26 Jan sits inside their 27 Jan–2 Feb Byron/Gold Coast window only by a day, so it needs the arrival pulled forward 24 hours.
why_rated: A free, walk-up Australia Day option with a real programme rather than a pub — outdoor stage, arts precinct, riverfront, fireworks. Cheapest credible way to honour the Australia Day soft anchor on the east coast.

name: Scenic Rim — Mount Barney, Main Range & Queen Mary Falls
season_note: Mount Barney is a serious unmarked scramble and summer is the wrong time — heat exhaustion is the standard rescue callout, and afternoon storms on an exposed ridge are genuinely dangerous. The lower-altitude bits (Queen Mary Falls at Killarney, Cunninghams Gap short walks, Lake Moogerah) stay fine and are green and full in the wet.
why_rated: The unfashionable inland arc between the Gold Coast and Toowoomba — World Heritage rainforest, an 1,100m granite peak that hikers rate as SE QLD's hardest day, and farm-stay country with almost no international traffic. Forum 'hidden gem' threads keep returning to it.

name: Noosa National Park coastal walk & Noosa Heads
season_note: The walk itself is perfect in summer if you go early; the town is not. January is Noosa's absolute peak — Hastings Street accommodation doubles or triples, the NP carpark is full by 7:30am, and a cheap bed in Noosa in January is close to a contradiction. Base in Noosaville/Sunshine Beach or day-trip in. No stingers this far south.
why_rated: The 5.4km headland track past Tea Tree Bay, Granite Bay, the Fairy Pools and Hell's Gates is free, koala-populated, and routinely called the best short coastal walk in Queensland. Add Australia's most reliable beginner point break at Noosa Main Beach — one of the very few north-facing, genuinely calm surf beaches in the country.

name: Noosa Everglades — kayak or boat the tea-tree waterways
season_note: Dec–Jan is the busiest season, so book ahead; guided boat tours from Noosaville start around A$90pp for 2.5 hours, self-hire kayaks are far cheaper. Summer means mirror-flat mornings and storms by 3pm — go on the early departure. Bring insect repellent; the tea-tree channels breed mosquitoes.
why_rated: One of only two everglades systems on Earth: 60km of tannin-stained water so still it mirrors the sky perfectly, tea-tree infused swimming, and a wilderness that starts 20 minutes from a resort town. The 'Noosa nobody photographs'.

name: Glass House Mountains & Mount Ngungun
season_note: Free, but the summer heat is the whole problem — Mt Ngungun is a 2.8km return climb on exposed rock and rangers see heat cases every January. Start at first light or do the drive-and-lookout version (Glass House Mountains Lookout, Wild Horse Mountain) instead. Trails close after heavy rain.
why_rated: Thirteen volcanic plugs erupting out of flat pineapple country, National Heritage listed and sacred to the Gubbi Gubbi. Mt Ngungun is the accessible one — 253m, a clear graded track, and a summit view of Tibrogargan and Beerwah that people call the best cheap thrill on the Sunshine Coast.

name: Blackall Range loop — Maleny, Montville, Kondalilla, Mary Cairncross
season_note: Range altitude keeps it several degrees cooler than the coast and Kondalilla Falls actually runs in the wet — summer is arguably the best time for this loop. Rock pools are swimmable but slippery; the falls track closes after very heavy rain. Maleny's Sunday market and Montville's galleries are open year-round.
why_rated: Maleny is the Sunshine Coast's alternative-culture town — food co-op, community-owned credit union, organic growers, buskers — and Montville is the twin village of craft galleries next door. Kondalilla's 90m falls and swimming holes and the Mary Cairncross rainforest reserve with its Glass House Mountains panorama complete a loop people rate as the best drive in SE QLD.

name: Mooloolaba, Coolum & Caloundra beach strip
season_note: Right season, wrong prices: January is school-holiday peak and Sunshine Coast accommodation is at its annual maximum. Book far ahead or stay inland at Nambour/Palmwoods and drive in. Patrolled beaches, no stingers, warm water — the actual swimming is excellent.
why_rated: The cheaper, less self-conscious alternative to Noosa: Mooloolaba's Spit and patrolled beach, the Coolum boardwalk and Mount Coolum's 30-minute summit climb, Point Cartwright's headland, and Caloundra's Bulcock Beach and Pumicestone Passage. Locals rate this strip above Noosa for value.

name: Rainbow Beach, Carlo Sandblow & Double Island Point
season_note: Good swimming and warm water, but the coloured-sand cliffs and sandblow are brutal at midday in January (no shade, reflected heat) — sunrise or sunset only. Beach driving is tide-locked, not date-locked: the Teewah/Great Beach Drive run must be done on a falling tide, and 4WD hire adds A$200+/day. Cyclone swell can close Double Island Point.
why_rated: The 600m walk to Carlo Sandblow ends on a 15-hectare dune with a 180° view over Rainbow Beach, the coloured sands, Double Island Point, K'gari and Inskip. Longboarders rate the Double Island Point right-hander as one of the longest waves in Australia, and the whole town is far cheaper and less packaged than Noosa an hour south.

name: Mary Valley — Kenilworth, Imbil & the Rattler steam railway
season_note: Green and lush in the wet; the Mary River swimming holes are at their best but can flood fast after storms. The Mary Valley Rattler heritage train runs on set days only (WEEKDAY-LOCKED — typically Wed/Sat/Sun, ~A$60–90pp) so check the timetable before committing a day.
why_rated: Dairy-and-hippie backcountry between Gympie and the Blackall Range — Kenilworth's famous cheese factory and giant yoghurt, the Borumba Deer Park festival site at Imbil, platypus in the Mary River, and a restored steam train through it. Almost no international traffic and consistently named on 'undiscovered Queensland' forum threads.

name: Jungle Love Festival, Imbil
season_note: ON HIATUS — the organisers' current line is 'we will return when the time is right', with no 2026 or 2027 dates announced. Historically a late-spring/early-summer boutique festival at Borumba Deer Park. Listed so it can be checked once rather than rediscovered.
why_rated: A beloved SEQ boutique festival on a creek — stages backing onto Yabba Creek so punters swim between sets, heavy on emerging local artists and art workers, small enough that people describe it as a friend's party. Exactly her kind of event if it ever returns to the calendar.

name: Brisbane city day — South Bank, Streets Beach, GOMA & the CityCat
season_note: January in Brisbane is hot and sticky (31°C, high humidity, near-daily late-afternoon storms) which is precisely why the free riverside lagoon exists. GOMA and the Queensland Museum are free and air-conditioned — the right move for a storm afternoon. The CityCat ferry is a normal-fare public transport ride, not a tour.
why_rated: The cheapest good day in the state: a free man-made beach and lagoon in the middle of a capital city, 17ha of riverside parkland with free BBQs, two major free-entry galleries (GOMA and QAG) that consistently out-programme Sydney's, and a river ferry that works as a A$5 harbour cruise.

name: Brisbane markets — Davies Park West End & Jan Powers
season_note: WEEKDAY-LOCKED: Davies Park Market (West End) Saturdays from 6am under the Moreton Bay figs; Jan Powers Farmers Markets rotate — Powerhouse New Farm on the 2nd and 4th Saturday, Brisbane City (Reddacliff Place) on Wednesdays; South Bank Collective Markets Fri evening–Sun. Go before 10am, it is 30°C+ by mid-morning.
why_rated: West End is Brisbane's counter-culture suburb and Davies Park is its weekly expression — organic growers, Vietnamese and Nepalese food stalls, buskers, secondhand and craft, under giant figs by the river. The single best cheap morning in Brisbane and squarely her scene.

name: Moreton Island (Mulgumpin) — Tangalooma Wrecks snorkel
season_note: Summer is the right season — warm water, best visibility on calm mornings, no tropical stingers this far south. Wind is the real risk: a strong sou'easter turns the wrecks into a washing machine and tours get cancelled. Day cruises run roughly A$121–192pp ex Holt Street Wharf; the sand-dune and 4WD version needs a vehicle barge.
why_rated: Fifteen deliberately scuttled ships in 2–10m of clear water, 40 minutes from Brisbane, holding 200+ fish species, 130 coral species, turtles, wobbegongs and rays — snorkellers call it the best shore-adjacent snorkel in southern Queensland. The world's third-largest sand island also offers desert sandboarding and wild dolphin feeding.

name: North Stradbroke Island (Minjerribah) — Gorge Walk & Point Lookout
season_note: Excellent summer destination — clear water, patrolled surf beaches, no tropical stingers. But January is peak local holiday season: campsites and the vehicle ferry book out weeks ahead. Passenger ferry from Cleveland from ~A$10 each way; vehicle ferry A$63.50–100 each way, so go without a car unless beach-camping. Beach camping needs a Vehicle Access Permit (PERMIT-LOCKED).
why_rated: The Gorge Walk at Point Lookout is a 1.2km clifftop loop where people routinely see turtles, manta rays, dolphins and (in season) whales from the boardwalk — plus kangaroos in the shade. Cylinder Beach, Brown Lake and Blue Lake round it out. Brisbane's own island, an hour from the CBD, and repeatedly named a national hidden gem.

name: Island Vibe Festival, Point Lookout (Minjerribah)
season_note: WRONG SEASON — Island Vibe runs 13–15 November 2026, six weeks before they arrive. No 2027 date announced. Captured because it is the best-fit festival on the SEQ calendar for her taste and worth knowing about for any future trip.
why_rated: A soul, reggae and dub festival held on the beachfront at Point Lookout on Quandamooka country — small, community-run, Indigenous-led, and set on one of the best beaches in south-east Queensland. Consistently the festival Brisbane's alternative scene names first.

name: Moreton Bay shore day — Bribie Island & Redcliffe
season_note: Calm bay water, warm, and reachable without a boat — Bribie is joined to the mainland by an 831m bridge and Redcliffe is 30 minutes from Brisbane on the train. Bay-side means little surf and sheltered swimming even when the coast is blown out by a summer storm. Jellyfish (harmless bay species) are more common in summer.
why_rated: The Brisbane locals' cheap beach day: Woorim's ocean surf on one side of Bribie and flat passage water on the other, plus Redcliffe's 22km of beachfront, the Sunday Redcliffe Jetty Markets and a peninsula that gets called 'Brisbane's little Maldives' by people who have clearly not been to the Maldives. Free, train-accessible, and almost never on a tourist itinerary.

name: Mount Coot-tha, Botanic Gardens & Story Bridge Adventure Climb
season_note: Mt Coot-tha lookout and the botanic gardens are free and best at sunrise or sunset — the middle of a January day is 32°C and glare. The Story Bridge climb is a paid adrenaline item (roughly A$140–160pp for the dawn/twilight climbs) and is cancelled in electrical storms, which January supplies most afternoons.
why_rated: Mt Coot-tha is Brisbane's highest point and the free city panorama everyone recommends; the adjacent botanic gardens hold a planetarium and a tropical dome. The Story Bridge climb is the only bridge climb in Australia besides Sydney's and costs roughly a third as much.

name: Brisbane Heat BBL at the Gabba (incl. New Year's Bash)
season_note: DATE-LOCKED: five Heat home games at the Gabba between 12 Dec 2026 and 17 Jan 2027, opening the BBL|16 season against the Sixers on Tue 15 Dec. The New Year's Bash v Hobart Hurricanes on 1 Jan 2027 is billed with a headline music act — but 1 Jan is the morning after the Sydney NYE hard anchor, so it is effectively unreachable.
why_rated: Cheap general-admission tickets, a three-hour night game in a legendary ground, beer and fireworks. Tagged sport: minor interest and a one-sided pick per the house rule — fine as a A$50–60 evening if they happen to be in Brisbane on a match night, never a reason to route through Brisbane.

name: Brisbane International tennis
season_note: DATE-LOCKED: 3–10 January 2027 at the Queensland Tennis Centre. Ground passes for the early rounds are the cheap way in and get you close to top-100 players on outside courts; finals tickets cost multiples of that. Falls squarely in the trip window but before the Cairns block.
why_rated: An Australian Open lead-in that attracts genuine ATP/WTA names at a fraction of Melbourne prices, on a compact site where a ground pass is decent value. Tagged sport: minor interest, his pick only — weight accordingly and never build a relocation around it.

name: Girraween National Park & the Granite Belt, Stanthorpe
season_note: One of the few inland Queensland places that is BETTER in summer — at 900m+ the Granite Belt runs 25–30°C days and 15°C nights while Brisbane bakes. Camping (~A$7.50pp/night national park rate) is comfortable. Caveats: the Pyramid's granite slab gets scorching by midday, and this is bushfire country in a dry summer.
why_rated: Giant balancing granite boulders, the Granite Arch, and The Pyramid — a bare rock dome you walk straight up for a view over the whole park. Next door is Australia's highest-altitude wine region with 40+ cellar doors and 55 wineries around Stanthorpe and Ballandean, all at country prices. The genuine 'why does nobody go here' entry for southern QLD.

name: Bunya Mountains
season_note: At 1,100m it is noticeably cooler than the Downs below and the rainforest walks stay pleasant in summer, but the access road is steep and fog-prone, and summer storms bring falling limbs. Dark skies are excellent when it is not overcast — which in January it often is.
why_rated: An island of ancient bunya pine rainforest marooned in dry farmland — grassy 'balds' full of wallabies at dusk, 35km of walking tracks, waterfalls, and deep cultural significance as the site of the historic Bunya nut gatherings that drew nations from across three states. Almost entirely domestic visitors.

name: Toowoomba — street art, Picnic Point & the escarpment
season_note: 700m altitude keeps it a few degrees below Brisbane, but the flagship Carnival of Flowers is September — WRONG SEASON, and the gardens Toowoomba is famous for are past their best by January. The First Coat street-art trail and the escarpment lookouts work year-round.
why_rated: An unlikely street-art city — dozens of large-scale murals through the CBD laneways from the First Coat festival — plus Picnic Point's escarpment view down the Lockyer Valley and the Table Top Mountain climb. Cheap beds and a real regional food scene; a natural first-night stop if driving inland from Brisbane.

name: K'gari (Fraser Island) — 4WD tag-along or guided tour
season_note: SUMMER CAUTIONS ARE REAL. January is peak dingo (wongari) risk — hot, hungry animals and school-holiday crowds produce most of the year's attack reports; never walk alone, never carry food, and fines apply for feeding. Add 33°C+ with no shade on 75 Mile Beach, marine stingers and sharks making the ocean unswimmable (you swim in the lakes only), and cyclone-season rain that can strand vehicles. Self-drive requires a Vehicle Access Permit and a barge booking (PERMIT-LOCKED). 2-day tag-along tours from Rainbow Beach/Hervey Bay run ~A$445pp.
why_rated: The world's largest sand island and a World Heritage site: Lake McKenzie's silica sand and perched freshwater, Eli Creek, the SS Maheno wreck, Pile Valley's rainforest growing straight out of sand, and 75 Mile Beach as a legal highway. Its 75 Mile Beach ranked third among Australia's hidden natural wonders. Genuinely spectacular — the season is the problem, not the place.

name: Hervey Bay
season_note: WRONG SEASON for the headline act — humpback whale watching in the Platypus Bay nursery runs July to October only, and that is the entire reason most people come. What remains in January: flat, sheltered, stinger-net-free bay swimming, the Urangan Pier, cheap accommodation, and the barge to K'gari. Hot and humid but the bay is protected from cyclone swell.
why_rated: In season, the world's most reliable place to be approached by curious humpbacks. Out of season it is simply a cheap, calm, unhurried bay town and the least painful K'gari launch point. Captured so the whale-season mismatch is recorded rather than rediscovered.

name: Mon Repos turtle rookery, Bundaberg
season_note: SEASON UNLOCK — this is one of the few Australian wildlife spectacles the trip's dates actively enable. Nesting runs Nov–Mar; HATCHLINGS emerge late January to end of March. From late Jan to late Feb both nesting and hatching happen and your group is walked to whichever is happening. Tours are ranger-led, nightly, ticketed through QLD Parks and sell out — 2026/27 tickets went on sale 1 June 2026, so BOOK EARLY. Tours run late into the night; you wait until turtles appear.
why_rated: The largest concentration of nesting loggerheads in the South Pacific and the most significant loggerhead rookery in the southern hemisphere, on a suburban beach outside Bundaberg. Watching a nest boil over with hatchlings racing to the sea is routinely called one of the world's great wildlife experiences — and it is a A$50-ish ranger tour, not a A$500 boat.

name: Lady Musgrave Island day cruise (Southern Great Barrier Reef)
season_note: The southern reef has NO tropical stingers — a real advantage over Cairns in January, where you snorkel in a lycra suit. Summer is also green-turtle nesting and hatching season on the cay. Against it: cyclone-season swell cancels sailings, the 90-minute catamaran crossing can be rough, and manta season is May–September. Expect ~A$250pp plus a fuel levy (~A$16.75) and a A$11 national park fee each.
why_rated: A genuine coral cay inside a 3,000-acre turquoise lagoon at the southern end of the Great Barrier Reef — you can walk the island, snorkel from the beach, and share the water with turtles, reef sharks and clouds of fish with a fraction of the Cairns crowd. Forum consensus on the Brisbane–Cairns drive names this the most underrated reef access in the state. NOTE: overlaps the already-researched GBR capsule — treat as the budget southern alternative, not a duplicate.

name: Lady Elliot Island day trip (scenic flight)
season_note: Stinger-free southern reef and peak green/loggerhead turtle nesting and hatching season on the island. But the marquee manta aggregation is May–September, humpbacks are May–November, and the day-trip price (roughly A$800–900 per person including the light-aircraft flight from Bundaberg/Hervey Bay) makes it one of the most expensive single days available anywhere on this trip.
why_rated: A coral cay at the southern tip of the reef with visibility regularly over 20m, snorkelling straight off the beach into resident turtles and reef sharks, and a bird rookery. Divers rate it in the top handful of Australian sites. Included as a known splurge — the couple can weigh it against a Cairns reef day at a third of the price.

name: Agnes Water & Town of 1770
season_note: Right season: warm water, southernmost surf beach in Queensland, no tropical stingers. January is Australian holiday season so the campgrounds fill, but it never gets Noosa-level busy. Summer storms and the occasional cyclone swell close the bar; sandflies at dusk are relentless.
why_rated: Repeatedly named the most underrated stop on the entire Brisbane–Cairns run — a tiny twin-town with the last surf beach before the reef blocks the swell, a west-facing headland at 1770 that gives you a sunset OVER the water on the east coast, and cheap surf lessons for beginners. Amphibious LARC tours to Bustard Head Lighthouse run A$45 (1hr) to A$179 (full day with lunch and sandboarding).

name: Great Keppel Island & Yeppoon
season_note: Warm water and fringing reef right off the sand, but this is just inside the tropical stinger zone — box jellyfish are a genuine January risk on mainland and island beaches here, so full-body lycra or netted areas only. Half the island's resort infrastructure has been derelict for years, which is why it is cheap. Ferry ~30 min from Yeppoon; cyclone risk.
why_rated: Seventeen white-sand beaches, snorkel-off-the-beach hard and soft coral, turtles and manta rays, and camping permitted — an almost-empty tropical island for a fraction of Whitsundays money. Yeppoon on the mainland has a free foreshore lagoon and cheap beds. The most consistently named 'why is nobody here' island in Queensland.

name: Capricorn Caves & Mount Archer, Rockhampton
season_note: A rare summer-proof activity in a very hot town — Rockhampton regularly tops 35°C in January but the limestone caves are cool and shaded. Cathedral Cave walking tours are the easy option; adventure caving and abseiling cost more and involve squeezes. Mount Archer's skywalk is best at sunset.
why_rated: Privately run limestone caves above ground (not below it) with a natural cathedral chamber used for concerts and famous acoustics, plus a December solstice light beam. Rockhampton is a functional overnight stop on the coastal drive with a free zoo and botanic gardens; the caves are what make the stop worth planning.

name: Carnarvon Gorge
season_note: SUMMER IS THE WRONG TIME AND THE PARK SAYS SO. The 87km Carnarvon Great Walk is CLOSED outside 1 March–31 October. The gorge campground opens only during Queensland school holidays. Summer brings extreme heat on a 20km day walk with river crossings, plus flash-flood risk in a slot gorge and unsealed access roads that cut after rain. May–September is the season; June–July is ideal at 25–27°C.
why_rated: Australia's most spectacular sandstone gorge system — white cliffs, cycads and king ferns, the Amphitheatre slot chamber reached by ladder, Ward's Canyon, and some of the finest Aboriginal stencil rock art in the country at the Art Gallery and Cathedral Cave. It is a genuine bucket-list Queensland destination that this trip simply cannot do properly.

name: Cape Hillsborough sunrise kangaroos
season_note: The kangaroos come out year-round, but summer sunrise is around 5am — you must be ON the beach before first light or the mob is gone. Also inside the tropical stinger zone, so no ocean swimming without lycra. Wet-season rain can wash out the beach access; the ranger-guided eco-tour (small fee) is the reliable version.
why_rated: Eastern grey kangaroos and wallabies feeding on the sand at dawn with the sun coming up over island silhouettes — one of the most photographed and least-visited wildlife scenes in Australia, 20 minutes north of Mackay. Every guide warns that arriving even 15 minutes late means an empty beach, which tells you how brief and how real it is.

name: Eungella NP platypus & Finch Hatton Gorge
season_note: Platypus viewing at Broken River works year-round at dawn and dusk, but heavy wet-season rain muddies the water and drops sighting rates; the Finch Hatton Gorge swimming holes are conversely at their best. The gorge road has several causeways that flood, and the range road up to Eungella is steep and fog-bound. Leeches after rain.
why_rated: The single most reliable place in Australia to see a wild platypus — a purpose-built viewing platform on Broken River where they surface most mornings — plus Australia's longest stretch of continuous subtropical rainforest and the Araluen and Wheel of Fire cascades at Finch Hatton. Almost nobody detours off the Bruce Highway for it.

name: Whitehaven Beach & Hill Inlet day trip from Airlie Beach
season_note: January is stinger season in the Whitsundays — box jellyfish and Irukandji are present and every operator issues full-body lycra suits; Whitehaven swimming is stinger-suit-only, which takes the edge off the fantasy. Add cyclone season (Debbie in 2017 flattened Airlie), afternoon storms and 32°C with high humidity. Day tours run roughly A$139–188pp; a sailing day from ~A$235pp. Airlie's free stinger-netted lagoon is the compensation.
why_rated: 98% pure silica sand that squeaks and stays cool underfoot, and the swirling tidal sandbars of Hill Inlet from Tongue Point — the most photographed beach in Australia and one of very few that live up to it. NOTE: deliberately framed as the beach/sailing day, NOT as reef access — the Whitsundays-as-reef-base capsule is already researched.

name: Bowen — Horseshoe Bay & the Big Mango
season_note: Beautiful but inside the stinger zone — Horseshoe Bay has no permanent net and box jellyfish/Irukandji make November–May swimming a lycra-suit affair. Also directly in the cyclone corridor. Cheap beds and near-empty beaches are the trade-off.
why_rated: A working mango-and-tomato town with a string of small granite-framed coves (Horseshoe Bay, Murrays Bay, Rose Bay) that people rate above anything at Airlie, snorkelling straight off the sand, a Baz Luhrmann film-set history, and a genuinely absurd 10-metre fibreglass mango. The definition of an underrated Bruce Highway stop.

name: Magnetic Island — Forts Walk, koalas & Horseshoe Bay
season_note: The island is fine year-round but January is the hard month: the Forts Walk track is exposed and rangers advise early morning or late afternoon only in summer, and the beaches are inside the stinger zone (netted enclosures at Picnic Bay, Horseshoe Bay and Nelly Bay are the safe swims). 30-minute ferry from Townsville. Cyclone risk.
why_rated: Over 800 wild koalas — the largest wild colony in northern Australia — and the 2km Forts Walk to WWII gun emplacements is the single most reliable place in the country to see one dozing above the track, with 360° sea views thrown in. Rock wallabies hand-feed at Geoffrey Bay, hostels and cabins keep it cheap, and locals hire open-top Barbie cars to get around.

name: Townsville — Castle Hill, The Strand & Riverway
season_note: Townsville is the driest tropical city in Queensland — it gets a fraction of Cairns' rainfall, so it is a better wet-season bet than the coast further north. Still 32°C and humid; the Castle Hill goat track is a sunrise-only proposition in January. Strand swimming is inside stinger enclosures November–May. Cyclone risk.
why_rated: A pink granite monolith in the middle of a city that 2,500 locals climb daily for a 360° view; a 2.2km beachfront promenade with free rock pools, netted swimming and public BBQs; and the free Riverway lagoons. Repeatedly called the most underrated stop on the Brisbane–Cairns drive — a real city rather than a resort strip, with prices to match.

name: Wallaman Falls, Girringun NP (Ingham)
season_note: The wet season is when it is at its most spectacular — a 268m drop needs water and January delivers it. The catch: the last stretch of access road is steep, winding and closes in heavy rain, and the 3.2km Djyinda track down to the base is a punishing climb back out in 90% humidity. Camping permit ~A$7.50pp/night.
why_rated: Australia's highest permanent single-drop waterfall — Stony Creek falling 268m clear into a rainforest plunge pool west of Ingham. Almost everyone drives past on the Bruce Highway without knowing it exists, and it is one of the few Queensland attractions genuinely improved by the wet season.

name: Hinchinbrook Island — Thorsborne Trail
season_note: PERMIT-LOCKED and wrong season. The trail caps numbers hard (a few dozen walkers on the island at a time) and permits sell out months out; camping is A$7.50pp/night plus boat transfers both ends. December–March is the wet: creek crossings become impassable, humidity is extreme, estuarine crocodiles are active in the creek mouths, and the recommended hiking season is April–September. Cyclones close it outright.
why_rated: 32km over four days along the east coast of Australia's largest island national park — no roads, no facilities, rainforest to mangrove to empty beach, Zoe Falls, and a walk consistently ranked among the country's great multi-day treks. Recorded honestly as out of reach for this trip.

name: Mission Beach — skydive & Dunk Island
season_note: Mission Beach is one of the wettest places in Australia and January is its wettest month — the beach-landing skydive (~A$272pp from 15,000ft) is weather-cancelled often in the wet, and cloud ruins the view when it does run. The 14km of beach is inside the stinger zone with a small netted enclosure only, and this stretch takes direct cyclone hits (Larry, Yasi). Dunk Island water-taxi half-days from ~A$108pp.
why_rated: The rainforest meets the beach with no development in between, and the skydive is famous for landing on the sand with the reef and Dunk Island below you — routinely called the most scenic drop zone in Australia. Note: the cassowary angle here is already covered by the researched FNQ capsule; this entry is the beach/adventure half.

name: Tully River white-water rafting
season_note: SEASON UNLOCK — the Tully is dam-released so it runs year-round, but the wet season adds natural flow and the rapids get bigger and faster in January. That is a plus for the ride and a minus for nerves; operators upgrade grades after heavy rain and occasionally cancel at flood levels. Around A$150pp all-inclusive with transfers from Mission Beach, more from Cairns. Leeches and rain are part of the day.
why_rated: Grade 3–4 rapids through a rainforest gorge in Australia's wettest catchment, 45 minutes inland from Mission Beach — the country's most consistently recommended commercial rafting river, and one of the few adventure activities that genuinely improves in a Queensland January.

name: Paronella Park, Mena Creek
season_note: Better in the wet — Mena Creek Falls, which the whole park is built around, actually thunders in January, and the moss and vines that make the ruins look enchanted need the rain. Ticket includes a night tour and the entry is valid for multiple days. Hot, humid and mosquito-heavy; the paths get slick.
why_rated: A Spanish immigrant spent the 1930s hand-building a mock castle, ballroom, tennis courts and grand staircase in the rainforest beside a waterfall, powered by his own hydro plant; cyclones and fire have half-reclaimed it. The night tour with the ruins lit is the bit people rave about. Pure Queensland eccentricity and completely unlike anything else on the coast.

name: Babinda Boulders & Josephine Falls
region: QLD — Wooroonooran NP / south of Cairns
season_note: SAFETY FLAG — both are wet-season death traps at exactly this time of year. Josephine Falls' granite water slide becomes dangerous after rain and the pool floods fast; Devil's Pool at Babinda has killed many people and swimming below the boulders is banned outright. Water levels rise in minutes during a storm upstream even when it is sunny where you stand. In dry spells they are superb; in January, check conditions, obey the signs, and swim only in the designated calm area at Babinda.
why_rated: The two most famous freshwater swimming holes in Far North Queensland — clear granite-bottomed pools in rainforest, free, twenty minutes off the highway, and the standard local answer to 'where do you swim during stinger season'. They belong in the catalog with the danger stated plainly rather than left out.

name: Atherton Tablelands waterfall circuit (Millaa Millaa, Zillie, Ellinjaa)
season_note: SEASON UNLOCK — the falls are fullest during and just after the wet, and the Tablelands sit 700–900m up, so it runs 5–8°C cooler than Cairns. This is the standard local answer to 'what do I do in Cairns when it rains'. Caveats: swimming holes can be closed after heavy rain, the circuit road has blind corners, and Millaa Millaa is busy at midday because of the shampoo-ad photo.
why_rated: A 16km loop road linking three waterfalls, of which Millaa Millaa is the most photographed in Australia — a perfect curtain into a swimmable pool. The whole Tablelands drive (Malanda, Mungalli, Nandroya) is dairy-and-rainforest country an hour from the reef and half the price.

name: Yungaburra — Curtain Fig, platypus & the monthly market
season_note: Platypus at the Peterson Creek platform work at dawn and dusk year-round; heavy wet-season rain lowers the odds but sightings continue. DATE-LOCKED market: Yungaburra Markets run the fourth Saturday of each month, 7:30am–12:30pm, ~250 growers and artisans — that is 23 Jan 2027, which sits inside their Cairns block (18–31 Jan). Cool nights at 750m.
why_rated: A heritage timber village that is the Tablelands' alternative-culture hub, one of the most reliable wild platypus spots in Australia (a free viewing platform in walking distance of the pub), and the 500-year-old Curtain Fig — aerial roots hanging in a 15m curtain, floodlit at night, a two-minute walk from the carpark. Cheap, unhurried, and a natural counterweight to a big reef day.

name: Crater Lakes — Lake Eacham & Lake Barrine
season_note: One of the best January answers in Far North Queensland: volcanic crater lakes with no crocodiles, no stingers and no current — genuinely safe, free freshwater swimming during stinger season. Cool (they sit at altitude) and shaded. Rain makes the rainforest circuit walks muddy and leechy but does not affect the swim.
why_rated: Two water-filled maar craters ringed by rainforest — Lake Eacham has a sandy entry, a pontoon and a 3km lakeside circuit, and turtles come to you; Lake Barrine has a century-old teahouse and two giant kauri pines. The default local move when the coast is closed for stingers, and it costs nothing.

name: Cairns city — Esplanade Lagoon, Rusty's Markets & Night Markets
season_note: The Esplanade Lagoon exists because you cannot swim in Cairns — the foreshore is mudflats with crocodiles and, November–May, box jellyfish and Irukandji. The free saltwater lagoon is lifeguarded and open year-round and is the single most-used facility in the city in January. WEEKDAY-LOCKED: Rusty's Markets Fri and Sat 5am–4pm, Sun 5am–3pm. Night Markets nightly.
why_rated: Rusty's has traded since 1975 and is the real thing — Far North growers, Asian herbs, tropical fruit you have never seen, and cheap cooked food, in a covered CBD block. Add a free lagoon, an esplanade boardwalk full of shorebirds, and the Tanks Arts Centre in old WWII fuel tanks. The cheapest good day in Cairns and all of it survives a downpour.

name: Fitzroy Island
season_note: 45 minutes from Cairns and inside the stinger zone — Nudey Beach has a seasonal net and the resort supplies lycra suits; snorkelling in January is a stinger-suit activity. Wet-season runoff cuts visibility on the fringing reef after big rain. Cyclone risk. Camping and a hostel-tier bunkhouse keep the budget version alive. Overlaps the researched reef capsule — this is the cheap, no-boat-day version.
why_rated: A continental island with rainforest to the waterline, a fringing reef you snorkel straight off the sand at Nudey Beach (repeatedly voted Australia's best beach), a summit walk with reef views, and a turtle rehabilitation centre you can tour. The lowest-cost way to get reef-adjacent water out of Cairns.

name: Kuranda & Port Douglas market days
season_note: WEEKDAY-LOCKED, and this is the whole point of the entry: Kuranda's Original Rainforest Markets and Heritage Markets both run Wednesday to Sunday only (closed Mon–Tue); Port Douglas Markets are Sunday 8am–1:30pm on the Dickson Inlet foreshore. Both are open-air and shaded but January humidity means going before 10am. NOTE: the Kuranda Scenic Railway/Skyrail capsule is already researched — this entry is the market-day scheduling constraint, not a duplicate of the transport experience.
why_rated: Kuranda's markets are the surviving descendant of a 1970s hippie village market — leatherwork, didgeridoos, crystals, tie-dye, opals and the region's alternative-culture crowd, in a rainforest town. Port Douglas Markets are widely called the best on the northern coast for local produce, craft and jewellery, in a park under mango trees on the water.

name: Chillagoe caves & smelters
region: QLD — Far North Queensland / Gulf Savannah
season_note: Explicitly recommended by tour operators as the SUMMER SUBSTITUTE for Undara, which closes Nov–Feb — Chillagoe stays open. But it is a 3.5-hour drive west of Cairns into dry outback that hits 38–40°C in January, the last stretch is narrow and can cut in the wet, and there is very little in town. Ranger-guided cave tours are cool inside and cheap; day tours from Cairns are long.
why_rated: Limestone karst towers erupting out of red savannah, ranger-led caves with formations and bat colonies, ruined 1900s copper smelter stacks, and Aboriginal rock art — an outback frontier town three hours from a reef resort. The strangest day trip available from Cairns and one almost no visitor makes.

name: Undara Lava Tubes
season_note: CLOSED FOR THE TRIP WINDOW — the lava tubes operate March to October only and are shut November through February. Access is by guided tour exclusively (Adult A$120, tours 9:30am and 1:30pm in season). Operators point summer visitors to Chillagoe instead. Recorded so it can be crossed off once.
why_rated: The longest lava tube system from a single volcano on Earth — 190,000-year-old collapsed basalt tunnels you walk through, with a Savannah Guide interpreting, plus accommodation in restored railway carriages and a bat exodus at dusk. A genuine world-class geological site that this trip's dates simply lock out.

name: Cooktown & the Mulligan Highway
season_note: ROUTE-LOCKED BY THE WET. The scenic coastal option — the Bloomfield Track through Cape Trib — is 4WD-only and closes for extended periods without notice November–April. The inland sealed Mulligan Highway (331km, ~4.5 hours) stays viable for most of the wet and is the only sensible self-drive option in January, and even that needs a road-conditions check. Add 34°C, extreme humidity, crocodiles in every waterway, and cyclone risk this far north.
why_rated: Grassy Hill Lookout was ranked fifth among Australia's top hidden natural wonders — Cook careened the Endeavour here in 1770 and the town has been quietly decaying and reinventing ever since. The James Cook Museum, the Nature's Powerhouse botanic gardens, Black Mountain's boulder field on the way in, and the Guugu Yimithirr history that produced the word 'kangaroo'. The end of the sealed road north.

name: Longreach — Qantas Founders Museum & Stockman's Hall of Fame
season_note: HEAT WARNING — Longreach is explicitly recommended for April–September; January routinely runs 38–42°C and the tarmac-wing walk over the 747 and 707 is done in full sun. Summer also thins the programme: the Qantas Founders light show drops to twice a week with a six-person minimum. Wet-season storms can cut unsealed roads. Everything worth doing is indoors or at dawn.
why_rated: Qantas was born out here — the museum holds a 747 and a 707 you can walk on and inside, and the Australian Stockman's Hall of Fame next door is the national museum of pastoral Australia. Add Thomson River sunset cruises and Cobb & Co coach rides. This is the outback-Queensland experience most people actually mean, and the heat is the only thing standing in the way.

name: Winton — Australian Age of Dinosaurs & the Dinosaur Stampede
season_note: HEAT WARNING — guides recommend Winton in June–August and warn off spring and summer; January is 38–42°C on an exposed mesa with the Dinosaur Canyon outdoor galleries in full sun. Allow three hours minimum for the three facilities, all of which involve walking outside between them. Roads to Lark Quarry are partly unsealed and cut after wet-season rain.
why_rated: The world's largest collection of Australian dinosaur fossils, on a 'jump-up' mesa above the Mitchell grass, with a working fossil-prep lab you watch. Lark Quarry preserves the only recorded dinosaur stampede trackway on Earth. Winton is also where Waltzing Matilda was first performed and where Qantas held its first board meeting — an absurd amount of Australian mythology in one 900-person town.

name: Porcupine Gorge & Charters Towers
season_note: HEAT WARNING — 'Australia's Little Grand Canyon' sits in dry inland country that runs 38°C+ in January, and the only real walk is a steep 1.2km descent to the Pyramid and back out, unshaded. The waterhole at the bottom is the reward and is at its fullest after wet-season rain, which also cuts access roads. Best April–September.
why_rated: A 120m sandstone gorge cut through basalt with a striped rock pyramid and a permanent waterhole, 60km north of Hughenden, with a clifftop campground and almost no other people. Charters Towers on the way is a preserved 1870s gold-rush city that was briefly Queensland's second largest — the pair make a proper three-day inland loop from Townsville.

name: Boodjamulla (Lawn Hill) Gorge & Riversleigh fossil fields
region: QLD — North West Outback / Gulf Country
season_note: CLOSED. Boodjamulla shuts for the wet season every year — the 2025/26 closure ran 15 December to 3 April, and the 2026/27 dates will mirror it. Access is hundreds of kilometres of unsealed road that becomes impassable, and the park has already had a multi-year closure after 2023 flooding. Absolutely not available in the trip window.
why_rated: Emerald water in a red sandstone gorge you paddle by canoe, spring-fed and permanent in the middle of the Gulf, with the Riversleigh World Heritage fossil fields next door — one of the four richest mammal fossil sites on Earth. Frequently called Queensland's most spectacular national park. Recorded so it gets crossed off once, not researched twice.

name: Far outback QLD in summer — Birdsville, Mount Isa, Charleville, Karumba
region: QLD — Outback (Channel Country, Gulf, South West)
season_note: BLUNT NO for January. Birdsville and the Simpson Desert routinely exceed 45°C and the desert parks close to visitors over summer; the Birdsville Races are September. Gulf country (Karumba, Normanton, Burketown) is in the monsoon — roads cut for weeks, Gulf Developmental Road sections impassable, and the Morning Glory cloud is a September–November phenomenon. Mount Isa and Charleville are 40°C+. Charleville's Cosmos Centre dark-sky sessions are excellent but clouded out through the wet.
why_rated: Captured as one honest rejection rather than five separate ones. The famous stuff — the Birdsville Hotel and the Big Red dune, the Min Min lights at Boulia, the Cosmos Centre's telescopes under some of the darkest skies on Earth, barramundi and sunsets at Karumba, the underground mine tour at Mount Isa — is all real, and all is a dry-season (April–September) proposition. His road-trip nostalgia points this way; the calendar points hard against it.

name: Brisbane to Cairns coastal drive (Pacific Coast Way)
season_note: 1,390km and about 19 hours of driving; eight days is the commonly cited minimum and it is tight. January means wet-season driving from Townsville north (flooded causeways, the Bruce Highway cutting at Ingham and Cardwell in a big event), cyclone risk from Mackay north, and one-way campervan or car-hire relocation fees on top. Southbound in February would run against the worst of the monsoon.
why_rated: The spine that connects most of the other entries in this file — Noosa, Rainbow Beach, Bundaberg's turtles, 1770, Yeppoon, Cape Hillsborough, Airlie, Townsville, Magnetic Island, Mission Beach — and the format that best serves his road-trip nostalgia. Listed as a meta-capsule: toggling it on implies a whole run of the individual entries rather than duplicating them.
